Model Test-2.question: ১) What type of carditis is seen in acute rheumatic fever?
Model Test-2.exp:
The cardiac involvement in acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is classically pancarditis, meaning inflammation of all three layers of the heart:

  • Endocardium → Mainly affects valves (especially mitral valve) causing valvulitis and murmurs.

  • Myocardium → Causes myocarditis.

  • Pericardium → Causes pericarditis.

Other options:

  • Endocarditis → Only one component of rheumatic carditis, not the complete picture.

  • Myocarditis → A component but not the overall type.

  • Pericarditis → A component but not the overall type.

Exam pearl:
Acute rheumatic fever → Pancarditis (endocarditis + myocarditis + pericarditis).

Model Test-2.question: ২) What is the type of sputum in acute pulmonary edema?
Model Test-2.exp:
Explanation:
In acute pulmonary edema, the sputum is typically serous and frothy, often described as pink frothy sputum due to the presence of pulmonary capillary fluid with a small amount of blood.

Features of acute pulmonary edema:

  • Severe breathlessness

  • Orthopnea

  • Bilateral crepitations

  • Pink frothy/serous sputum

Other options:

  • Rusty sputum → Classically seen in pneumococcal pneumonia.

  • Purulent sputum → Suggests bacterial infection (e.g., bronchiectasis, lung abscess).

  • Mucoid sputum → Common in chronic bronchitis or asthma.

Exam pearl:
Acute pulmonary edema → Pink frothy (serous) sputum.

Model Test-2.question: ৩) Which is not a cause of chronic nonspecific gastritis?
Model Test-2.exp:
Chronic nonspecific gastritis is mainly caused by conditions affecting the gastric mucosa, especially:

  • H. pylori infection → Most common cause of chronic gastritis.

  • Autoimmune gastritis → Causes chronic atrophic gastritis, mainly affecting the body and fundus.

  • Post-gastrectomy → Can cause reflux gastritis due to bile reflux.

Crohn's disease is not a usual cause of chronic nonspecific gastritis. Although Crohn’s disease can involve the stomach (gastroduodenal Crohn’s), it is uncommon and not classified as a typical cause of chronic nonspecific gastritis.

Exam pearl:
Chronic gastritis causes → H. pylori + autoimmune + bile reflux (post-gastrectomy).

Model Test-2.question: ৪) What is the cause of continuous murmur?
Model Test-2.exp:
A continuous murmur is classically seen in Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).

  • In PDA, there is a persistent connection between the descending aorta and pulmonary artery.

  • Blood flows continuously from the high-pressure aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole, producing a continuous “machinery” murmur.

Other options:

  • ASD → Causes a systolic ejection murmur with fixed split S2.

  • VSD → Causes a pansystolic murmur.

  • TOF (Tetralogy of Fallot) → Causes a systolic ejection murmur due to right ventricular outflow obstruction.

Exam pearl:
Continuous murmur → PDA (“machinery murmur”).

Model Test-2.question: ৫) Which lung vascular disease is responsible for hemoptysis?
Model Test-2.exp:
Pulmonary infarction is a lung vascular disease that can cause hemoptysis.

  • It occurs due to pulmonary embolism, causing ischemic necrosis of lung tissue.

  • The damaged pulmonary vessels may bleed into the airways, producing hemoptysis.

Other options:

  • Bronchial adenoma → A bronchial tumor that may cause hemoptysis but is not primarily a vascular disease.

  • Tuberculosis → Common cause of hemoptysis due to lung tissue destruction and cavitation, but not a vascular disease.

  • Actinomycosis → Chronic pulmonary infection that can cause hemoptysis, not a vascular disease.

Exam pearl:
Vascular causes of hemoptysis → Pulmonary embolism/infarction, pulmonary hypertension, AV malformations.

Model Test-2.question: ৬) Which is the most common complications of PUD?
Model Test-2.exp:
The most common complication of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is bleeding.

  • Ulcer erosion into underlying blood vessels (especially the gastroduodenal artery in duodenal ulcer) can cause upper GI bleeding.

  • Presentation may include hematemesis or melaena.

Other options:

  • Perforation → A serious complication but less common than bleeding.

  • Gastric outlet obstruction → Occurs due to chronic scarring and fibrosis, but is less frequent.

  • Gastric carcinoma → Not a complication of PUD; gastric cancer is a separate disease (though H. pylori is associated with both).

Exam pearl:
PUD complications (common → less common): Bleeding > Perforation > Gastric outlet obstruction.

Model Test-2.question: ৭) Which is not a cardinal feature of right heart failure?
Model Test-2.exp:
Orthopnea is not a cardinal feature of right heart failure; it is more commonly associated with left heart failure due to pulmonary congestion.

Features of right heart failure:

  • Dependent edema → Due to systemic venous congestion.

  • Raised JVP → Due to increased right atrial pressure.

  • Tender hepatomegaly → Due to hepatic venous congestion.

Other option:

  • Orthopnea  → Occurs in left ventricular failure because of increased pulmonary venous pressure and fluid redistribution when lying down.

Exam pearl:
Right heart failure → JVP ↑ + peripheral edema + tender hepatomegaly.
Left heart failure → Orthopnea + PND + pulmonary edema.

Model Test-2.question: ৮) Which one is a cause of Type-1 respiratory failure?
Model Test-2.exp:
Type-1 respiratory failure (hypoxemic respiratory failure) is characterized by:

  • Low PaO₂

  • Normal or low PaCO₂

  • Usually caused by problems with oxygenation, such as ventilation-perfusion mismatch or shunt.

Lung collapse (atelectasis) causes alveolar collapse and intrapulmonary shunting, leading to hypoxemia, so it is a cause of Type-1 respiratory failure.

Other options:

  • COPD → Typically causes Type-2 respiratory failure due to CO₂ retention.

  • Upper airway obstruction → Causes hypoventilation and CO₂ retention → Type-2 respiratory failure.

  • GBS (Guillain–Barré syndrome) → Respiratory muscle weakness causes hypoventilation → Type-2 respiratory failure.

Exam pearl:
Type-1 respiratory failure → Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, atelectasis.
Type-2 respiratory failure → COPD, neuromuscular disease, CNS depression.

Model Test-2.question: ৯) Which one is a criteria of cardiac chest pain?
Model Test-2.exp:
A typical cardiac chest pain (angina) is described as squeezing, pressure-like, or constricting discomfort.

Features of cardiac chest pain:

  • Central/retrosternal location

  • Tightness, pressure, heaviness, or squeezing sensation

  • May radiate to left arm, neck, jaw, or shoulder

  • Usually precipitated by exertion and relieved by rest

Other options:

  • Peripheral → Not typical; cardiac pain is usually central.

  • Localized → Suggests non-cardiac chest pain (e.g., musculoskeletal).

  • No radiation → Cardiac pain commonly has radiation, though it may sometimes be absent.

Exam pearl:
Typical angina = Retrosternal squeezing pain + radiation + exertional relation + relief with rest.

Model Test-2.question: ১০) Fever with drenching night sweat occurs in which of the following condition?
Model Test-2.exp:
Drenching night sweats with fever is a classic B symptom of lymphoma.

B symptoms of lymphoma include:

  • Unexplained fever

  • Drenching night sweats

  • Unintentional weight loss

Other options:

  • Encephalitis → Causes fever with neurological symptoms, not typically drenching night sweats.

  • Meningitis → Causes fever, headache, neck stiffness, but night sweats are not a classic feature.

  • Enteric fever → Causes prolonged fever, but drenching night sweats are not characteristic.

Exam pearl:
Lymphoma B symptoms = Fever + Drenching night sweats + Weight loss.

Model Test-2.question: ১১) Absolute contraindication for upper GIT endoscopy is..?
Model Test-2.exp:
The absolute contraindication for upper GI endoscopy (OGD) among the given options is severe shock.

  • Severe shock is an absolute contraindication because the patient is hemodynamically unstable and sedation/endoscopy can worsen cardiovascular compromise.

Other options:

  • Severe respiratory disease → Relative contraindication; procedure may be done with caution and proper monitoring.

  • Atlanto-axial subluxation → Relative contraindication due to risk during neck extension/intubation (especially in Down syndrome).

  • Recent MI → Relative contraindication; endoscopy may be performed if benefits outweigh risks.

Exam pearl:
Upper GI endoscopy contraindications:

  • Absolute → Severe shock, patient refusal, suspected perforation (unless therapeutic indication).

  • Relative → Severe cardiopulmonary disease, recent MI, cervical spine instability.

Model Test-2.question: ১২) Which one is a cause of bilateral pleural effusion?
Model Test-2.exp:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a common cause of bilateral pleural effusion due to lupus pleuritis.

  • SLE can cause inflammation of the pleura leading to exudative pleural effusion, often affecting both sides.

Other options:

  • Liver abscess → Usually causes right-sided pleural effusion due to diaphragmatic irritation (especially amoebic liver abscess).

  • Pancreatitis → Can cause pleural effusion, often left-sided, due to pancreatic inflammation or pancreaticopleural fistula.

  • Pulmonary infarction → Usually causes a small unilateral pleural effusion.

Exam pearl:
Bilateral pleural effusion causes → SLE, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis.

Model Test-2.question: ১৩) All of the following are causes of right heart failure except....?
Model Test-2.exp:
Aortic stenosis (AS) is not a cause of right heart failure.

Right heart failure commonly occurs due to conditions that increase pulmonary circulation pressure or cause right ventricular volume overload.

Other options:

  • MS (Mitral stenosis) → Causes pulmonary hypertension → increased RV workload → right heart failure.

  • ASD (Atrial septal defect) → Causes right ventricular volume overload and may lead to right heart failure.

  • VSD (Ventricular septal defect) → Large VSD can cause pulmonary hypertension and eventually right heart failure (Eisenmenger syndrome).

Exam pearl:
Causes of right heart failure → MS, ASD, VSD, pulmonary hypertension, COPD.
Aortic stenosis → Mainly causes left ventricular pressure overload.

Model Test-2.question: ১৪) Usually amber colored pleural fluid is found in.....?
Model Test-2.exp:
Amber-colored pleural fluid is classically found in tuberculous pleural effusion.

  • TB pleural effusion is usually an exudative fluid with:

    • Straw-colored/amber appearance

    • High protein content

    • Increased lymphocytes

    • Raised ADA level

Other options:

  • Pneumonia → Usually produces turbid or purulent fluid (parapneumonic effusion/empyema).

  • Bronchial malignancy → Pleural fluid may be hemorrhagic or blood-stained.

  • Bronchiectasis → Usually associated with purulent sputum; pleural effusion is uncommon.

Exam pearl:
Amber/straw-colored pleural effusion + lymphocytosis → Think Tuberculosis.

Model Test-2.question: ১৫) Which one is a significant side effect of GTN?
Model Test-2.exp:
Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) is a nitrate drug that causes vasodilation by releasing nitric oxide (NO), leading to relaxation of vascular smooth muscle.

The most significant and common side effect is:

  • Throbbing headache → Due to cerebral vasodilation.

Other options:

  • Ototoxicity → Not associated with GTN.

  • Hyperglycemia → Not a typical adverse effect.

  • Hypouricaemia → Not a known significant side effect.

Exam pearl:
GTN adverse effects → Throbbing headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension, reflex tachycardia.

Model Test-2.question: ১৬) Which is the Tests of anatomy prior to surgery in chronic pancreatitis?
Model Test-2.exp:
The test of choice for assessing pancreatic duct anatomy prior to surgery in chronic pancreatitis is MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography).

  • MRCP is a non-invasive imaging technique that provides detailed visualization of the pancreatic duct and biliary tree.

  • It helps in planning surgery by identifying:

    • Ductal obstruction

    • Strictures

    • Duct dilatation

    • Stones

Other options:

  • ERCP → Previously used for duct imaging but now mainly therapeutic because it is invasive and carries risk of pancreatitis.

  • HR CT → Best for detecting pancreatic calcification and complications, but less detailed for duct anatomy.

  • MRI → Useful for pancreatic imaging, but MRCP is specifically designed for duct anatomy.

Exam pearl:
Chronic pancreatitis:

  • Duct anatomy before surgery → MRCP

  • Calcification → CT scan

  • Therapeutic duct intervention → ERCP.

Model Test-2.question: ১৭) Which is not true in case of clinical findings of pneumothorax?
Model Test-2.exp:
In pneumothorax, air accumulates in the pleural space, separating the lung from the chest wall. This reduces transmission of sound and vibration.

Clinical findings:

  • Hyper-resonant percussion note → Due to excess air in pleural space.

  • Breath sound diminished or absent → Due to reduced air entry.

  • Vocal fremitus reduced or absent → Sound vibrations are poorly transmitted through air.

Vocal resonance increased is not true because pleural air acts as a barrier and decreases sound transmission.

Exam pearl:
Pneumothorax → Hyper-resonance + ↓ breath sounds + ↓ vocal resonance + ↓ vocal fremitus.

Model Test-2.question: ১৮) Which drug is used in AF patient with MS?
Model Test-2.exp:
In a patient with atrial fibrillation (AF) associated with mitral stenosis (MS), digoxin is commonly used for rate control, especially when there is associated heart failure.

  • Mitral stenosis causes left atrial enlargement, predisposing to AF.

  • Rate control is important to improve ventricular filling and reduce symptoms.

Other options:

  • Beta blocker → Can be used for rate control in AF, but in MS with heart failure, digoxin is often preferred.

  • Diltiazem → Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for AF rate control, but not the classic choice in MS.

  • Verapamil → Also a rate-controlling drug, but less preferred in heart failure.

Exam pearl:
AF + Mitral stenosis → Digoxin (rate control) + anticoagulation (usually warfarin).

Model Test-2.question: ১৯) Which is not true about bronchial asthma?
Model Test-2.exp:
In bronchial asthma, patients usually have symptom-free intervals between attacks due to the variable and reversible nature of airway obstruction.

Features of bronchial asthma:

  • Positive history of allergy → Common, especially in atopic asthma.

  • Diurnal variation → Symptoms often worsen at night or early morning.

  • Normal CXR → Usually normal between attacks.

Other option:

  • Symptoms free interval absent → Not true; asthma typically has intermittent symptoms with symptom-free periods (except severe persistent asthma).

Exam pearl:
Asthma = Variable + reversible airway obstruction + symptom-free intervals + nocturnal/early morning worsening.

Model Test-2.question: ২০) Deficiency of which vitamin causes Korsakoff psycosis?
Model Test-2.exp:
Korsakoff psychosis is caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency.

  • It is commonly associated with chronic alcoholism.

  • Thiamine deficiency causes damage to areas of the brain involved in memory, especially:

    • Mammillary bodies

    • Medial thalamus

Clinical features:

  • Severe anterograde amnesia

  • Retrograde amnesia

  • Confabulation (fabrication of false memories)

Other options:

  • Riboflavin (B2) → Causes cheilosis, glossitis, dermatitis.

  • Niacin (B3) → Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).

  • Biotin (B7) → Causes dermatitis, alopecia.

Exam pearl:
Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency → Wernicke encephalopathy + Korsakoff psychosis.

Model Test-2.question: ২১) Which is not ECG criteria of SVT?
Model Test-2.exp:
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) typically shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia on ECG.

ECG criteria of SVT:

  • High heart rate (usually >150/min)

  • Narrow QRS complex (<120 ms)

  • Absent/hidden P waves or retrograde P waves

Irregular rhythm is not a typical feature of SVT. Irregular narrow-complex tachycardia suggests conditions like atrial fibrillation (AF) or atrial flutter with variable block.

Other options:

  • Absent P wave → Common in AVNRT (a common type of SVT).

  • Narrow QRS complex → Typical feature of SVT.

  • High heart rate → Defining feature of SVT.

Exam pearl:
SVT ECG = Regular rhythm + Narrow QRS + Fast rate + P wave absent/abnormal.

Model Test-2.question: ২২) what is the time required for hyperacute liver failure
Model Test-2.exp:
Hyperacute liver failure is the most rapid form of acute liver failure, defined by the development of hepatic encephalopathy within 7 days of the onset of jaundice (according to classic classification). However, in many exam classifications:

  • Hyperacute liver failure → Encephalopathy develops within <7 days (some sources further describe very rapid cases as <3 days).

  • Acute liver failure → Encephalopathy within 8–28 days.

  • Subacute liver failure → Encephalopathy within 5–12 weeks.

Given the options, the expected exam answer is:

✅ ক) <3 days

Other options:

  • <7 days → Also used in some modern definitions for hyperacute liver failure.

  • <15 days / <28 days → Not hyperacute; these fall into acute/subacute categories.

Exam pearl:
Hyperacute hepatic failure = very rapid encephalopathy (classically <7 days; exam keys may use <3 days).

Model Test-2.question: ২৩) In ECG of corpulmonale there will be feature of....?
Model Test-2.exp:
ECG features of cor pulmonale include:

  • Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

  • Right axis deviation (RAD)

  • P pulmonale (tall peaked P waves due to right atrial enlargement)

  • RBBB may

    Exam pearl:Cor pulmonale ECG → RVH + RAD + P pulmonale.

Model Test-2.question: ২৪) Which is not a feature of unstable angina?
Model Test-2.option1: occurs at rest or with minimal exertion
Model Test-2.exp:
Unstable angina is a form of acute coronary syndrome characterized by a change in the pattern of angina. The pain is typically more severe, prolonged, and unpredictable compared with stable angina.

Features of unstable angina:

  • Occurs at rest or with minimal exertion 

  • New onset angina (especially within weeks) 

  • Crescendo pattern (increasing frequency, severity, or duration) 

  • Chest pain usually lasts >10 minutes and may be prolonged 

Other option:

  • Lasting less than 10 mins → More typical of stable angina, where pain is brief and relieved by rest or GTN.

Exam pearl:
Unstable angina = Rest pain + New onset + Crescendo pattern + Duration usually >10 min.

Model Test-2.question: ২৫) Which is false about inspection finding in case of COPD?
Model Test-2.exp:
In COPD, the typical inspection findings are due to chronic airflow obstruction and hyperinflation.

Features of COPD:

  • Barrel-shaped chest  → Due to increased anteroposterior diameter from lung hyperinflation.

  • Pursed-lip breathing  → Helps prevent airway collapse during expiration.

  • Supraclavicular recession  → Due to increased work of breathing and use of accessory muscles.

  • Respiratory rate is usually increased (tachypnea)  → Not decreased.

Other option:

  • Decreased respiratory rate → Not a typical inspection finding of COPD; it may occur only in severe respiratory depression or CO₂ narcosis.

Exam pearl:
COPD inspection → Barrel chest + pursed-lip breathing + accessory muscle use + tachypnea.

Model Test-2.question: ২৬) ST elevation in MI signifies......?
Model Test-2.exp:
ST-segment elevation on ECG represents acute myocardial injury caused by transmural ischemia, where injured myocardial cells develop abnormal electrical potentials. It is the hallmark finding of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), usually due to complete coronary artery occlusion. However, ST elevation itself does not directly indicate necrosis; myocardial necrosis is confirmed by elevated cardiac biomarkers such as troponin. Myocardial ischemia typically causes ST depression or T-wave changes, while infarction is a clinical diagnosis requiring evidence of myocardial injury with necrosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • ST elevation → myocardial injury (acute phase)

  • Troponin elevation → myocardial necrosis

  • ST depression/T-wave inversion → ischemia

  • STEMI usually results from complete coronary artery occlusion

Exam Pearl:
ECG changes show myocardial injury; cardiac biomarkers confirm myocardial necrosis.

Model Test-2.question: ২৭) Which is not a sign of hepatic encephalopathy?
Model Test-2.exp:
Hepatic encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric complication of liver failure caused mainly by accumulation of neurotoxins such as ammonia, leading to altered brain function. Common neurological signs include asterixis (flapping tremor), constructional apraxia (difficulty copying or drawing figures), and bilateral extensor plantar responses in severe cases due to corticospinal tract involvement. Hyporeflexia is not a typical finding; reflexes are usually normal or exaggerated (hyperreflexia) in hepatic encephalopathy. Hyporeflexia suggests peripheral neuropathy or neuromuscular disorders rather than a central metabolic encephalopathy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Asterixis = classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy

  • Severe hepatic encephalopathy may show extensor plantar response

  • Reflexes are usually brisk, not reduced

  • Constructional apraxia indicates cortical dysfunction

Exam Pearl:
Hepatic encephalopathy causes asterixis with preserved or increased reflexes; hyporeflexia is not a feature.

Model Test-2.question: ২৮) What is the choice of investigation to confirm emphysema?
Model Test-2.exp:
The investigation of choice to confirm emphysema is high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest. HRCT provides detailed visualization of lung parenchyma and can detect characteristic features such as low-attenuation areas, destruction of alveolar walls, and distribution of emphysematous changes. Chest X-ray may show supportive findings like hyperinflation and flattened diaphragm but has lower sensitivity, especially in early disease. USG and MRI are not routinely used for diagnosing emphysema.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • HRCT chest = best imaging modality for emphysema confirmation

  • CXR findings: hyperinflation, increased retrosternal air space, flattened diaphragm

  • Emphysema = permanent destruction of alveolar walls with air-space enlargement

Exam Pearl:
HRCT is the most sensitive imaging test for confirming emphysematous changes.

Model Test-2.question: ২৯) In which MI heart failure is common?
Model Test-2.exp:
Heart failure is most commonly associated with anterior myocardial infarction because the anterior wall is supplied by the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. LAD occlusion often involves a large area of the left ventricle, including the interventricular septum and anterior wall, leading to significant loss of myocardial contractility and left ventricular dysfunction. Inferior, lateral, and posterior MIs may also cause heart failure, but the risk is generally lower due to smaller infarct size. Large anterior MI is a major predictor of acute left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Anterior MI (LAD occlusion) → highest risk of heart failure

  • Inferior MI (RCA occlusion) → commonly associated with bradycardia and AV block

  • Large infarct size → increased risk of LV dysfunction

Exam Pearl:
Anterior wall MI involving the LAD is the classic MI associated with heart failure.

Model Test-2.question: ৩০) Hyperthermia occurs when core temperature rises above.... oC?
Model Test-2.exp:
Hyperthermia is defined as an uncontrolled rise in core body temperature, usually when the core temperature exceeds 40°C. It occurs due to failure of thermoregulation, unlike fever where the hypothalamic set point is increased. Severe hyperthermia can cause cellular protein denaturation, neurological dysfunction, multiorgan failure, and death. Common causes include heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and serotonin syndrome. A normal core temperature is around 37°C, while temperatures above 40°C indicate a medical emergency requiring rapid cooling.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Hyperthermia → core temperature >40°C

  • Fever → raised hypothalamic set point

  • Heat stroke features: hyperthermia + CNS dysfunction

  • Malignant hyperthermia is associated with volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine

Exam Pearl:
Core temperature above 40°C with failed thermoregulation = hyperthermia.

Model Test-2.question: ৩১) Radio-opaque shadow with air Bronchogram is the characteristic CXR feature of......?
Model Test-2.exp:
A radio-opaque shadow with air bronchogram is a classic chest X-ray feature of pneumonia, especially lobar pneumonia. Consolidation of lung alveoli by inflammatory exudate increases the opacity of the affected area, while the air-filled bronchi remain visible as dark branching structures, producing an air bronchogram sign. Pulmonary hypertension shows enlarged pulmonary arteries, lung abscess typically shows a cavity with an air-fluid level, and bronchiectasis is characterized by bronchial dilation with tram-track or signet-ring appearances.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Air bronchogram → alveolar consolidation

  • Common in lobar pneumonia

  • Lung abscess → cavity + air-fluid level

  • Bronchiectasis → tram-track and signet-ring signs

    Exam Pearl:
    Air bronchogram on CXR strongly suggests lung consolidation, classically pneumonia.

Model Test-2.question: ৩২) Which is not a feature of innocent or benign murmur?
Model Test-2.exp:
Innocent (benign) murmurs are usually soft, occur during systole, have no significant radiation, and are commonly heard along the left sternal edge. A mid-diastolic murmur is not a feature of an innocent murmur and should raise suspicion for underlying structural heart disease, such as mitral stenosis or increased flow across valves. Innocent murmurs occur due to normal blood flow through structurally normal hearts and do not produce diastolic turbulence.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Innocent murmur: soft, systolic, localized, no radiation

  • Diastolic murmurs are always considered pathological until proven otherwise

  • Mitral stenosis → mid-diastolic rumbling murmur

Exam Pearl:
A diastolic murmur is pathological; innocent murmurs are systolic.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৩) Serum sickness, polyarthritis, glomerulonephritis along with usual features of acute viral hepatitis are present in hepatitis........ infection?
Model Test-2.exp:
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is classically associated with extrahepatic immune-mediated manifestations such as serum sickness-like syndrome, polyarthritis, and glomerulonephritis. These occur due to immune complex deposition involving viral antigens and antibodies, causing systemic inflammation. HBV can cause various renal diseases, including membranous nephropathy and polyarteritis nodosa. Hepatitis A and E are usually self-limiting acute infections with fewer extrahepatic immune complications, while hepatitis C is more commonly associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • HBV → serum sickness, polyarthritis, glomerulonephritis

  • HBV extrahepatic complication: polyarteritis nodosa

  • HCV → mixed cryoglobulinemia

  • Immune complex deposition is the underlying mechanism

Exam Pearl:
Serum sickness-like illness with arthritis in acute viral hepatitis strongly suggests Hepatitis B infection.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৪) CURB-65 score is the scoring system for assessment of severity of which disease?
Model Test-2.exp:
CURB-65 is a clinical scoring system used to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and guide decisions regarding hospitalization and treatment intensity. It includes five parameters: Confusion, Urea elevation, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, low Blood pressure, and age ≥65 years. A higher score indicates increased mortality risk and need for more aggressive management. It is not used for bronchial carcinoma, tuberculosis, or bronchiectasis severity assessment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • CURB-65 → Community-acquired pneumonia severity assessment

  • C = Confusion

  • U = Urea >7 mmol/L

  • R = Respiratory rate ≥30/min

  • B = Blood pressure low

  • 65 = Age ≥65 years

Exam Pearl:
CURB-65 is the standard severity scoring system for community-acquired pneumonia.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৫) What is the most dangerous complication of MI?
Model Test-2.exp:
The most dangerous early complication of myocardial infarction (MI) is ventricular fibrillation (VF) because it causes sudden cessation of effective cardiac output and can lead to sudden cardiac death if not immediately treated with defibrillation. VF is especially common within the first few hours after acute MI due to myocardial electrical instability. Cardiogenic shock is a serious complication associated with large infarctions, but VF is the most immediate life-threatening arrhythmia. AF and SVT are less commonly fatal complications of MI.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Early MI deaths are commonly due to ventricular arrhythmias

  • VF → most common cause of sudden cardiac death after MI

  • Cardiogenic shock → due to severe left ventricular pump failure

  • First-line treatment of VF → defibrillation

Exam Pearl:
After MI, ventricular fibrillation is the most immediately fatal complication.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৬) What is the duration of continuation phase of category-1 Regimen of anti-TB treatment?
Model Test-2.exp:
The Category-1 anti-tuberculosis regimen consists of an intensive phase followed by a continuation phase. The intensive phase is given for 2 months with HRZE (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol), followed by a continuation phase of 4 months with HR (Isoniazid and Rifampicin). Therefore, the total duration of the standard regimen is 6 months (2HRZE/4HR) for drug-susceptible tuberculosis. The continuation phase is important for eliminating remaining bacilli and preventing relapse.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Category-1 TB regimen: 2HRZE/4HR

  • Intensive phase → 2 months

  • Continuation phase → 4 months

  • Rifampicin and isoniazid are key sterilizing drugs

Exam Pearl:
Standard drug-sensitive TB treatment = 2 months intensive phase + 4 months continuation phase.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৭) Which is not a cardinal feature of ALVF?
Model Test-2.exp:
Acute left ventricular failure (ALVF) causes pulmonary venous congestion due to impaired left ventricular pumping, leading to symptoms and signs such as orthopnea, bilateral basal crepitations, and gallop rhythm (S3). Tender hepatomegaly is not a typical feature of ALVF; it is more commonly seen in right ventricular failure due to systemic venous congestion. In severe ALVF, pulmonary edema may occur, presenting with breathlessness, pink frothy sputum, and hypoxia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • LV failure → pulmonary congestion

  • Orthopnea → raised pulmonary venous pressure

  • S3 gallop → volume overload in heart failure

  • Tender hepatomegaly → right-sided heart failure

Exam Pearl:
Pulmonary signs indicate left heart failure; hepatomegaly indicates right heart failure.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৮) Which of the following is a feature of pyogenic liver abscess?
Model Test-2.exp:
Pyogenic liver abscess is commonly caused by bacterial infection and is often characterized by multiple abscesses, especially in patients with biliary tract infection or septicemia. The pus is typically thick and yellow-green, unlike amoebic liver abscess, which classically contains anchovy sauce-like pus. Pyogenic liver abscess is potentially serious and can be fatal if untreated, with complications such as sepsis and rupture. Therefore, the statement "less fatal" is incorrect. Since "all are true" is not correct, the best answer is multiple lesion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Pyogenic liver abscess → commonly multiple

  • Amoebic liver abscess → anchovy sauce pus

  • Pyogenic abscess → more systemic toxicity and higher mortality risk

  • Common organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus

Exam Pearl:
Anchovy sauce pus = amoebic abscess; multiple abscesses = pyogenic abscess.

Model Test-2.question: ৩৯) Gout can be an adverse effect of which anti-TB drug?
Model Test-2.exp:
Pyrazinamide can cause hyperuricemia and gout as an adverse effect. It inhibits renal tubular excretion of uric acid, leading to increased serum urate levels and precipitation of urate crystals in joints, causing acute gouty arthritis. This adverse effect is dose-related and more common during the intensive phase of tuberculosis treatment when pyrazinamide is included. Ethambutol may also rarely cause hyperuricemia, but pyrazinamide is the classic and most commonly tested association.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Pyrazinamide → hyperuricemia → gout

  • INH → peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis

  • Rifampicin → hepatotoxicity, orange discoloration of body fluids

  • Ethambutol → optic neuritis

Exam Pearl:
Among anti-TB drugs, pyrazinamide is the classic cause of gout due to hyperuricemia.

Model Test-2.question: ৪০) Which one corresponds to conjunctival xerosis in WHO classification of Xeropthalmia?
Model Test-2.exp:
In the WHO classification of xerophthalmia, X1A represents conjunctival xerosis, which is an early ocular manifestation of vitamin A deficiency. It occurs due to dryness and keratinization of the conjunctival epithelium. X2 indicates Bitot’s spots, X3A indicates corneal xerosis with corneal involvement of less than one-third, and X3B indicates corneal xerosis involving more than one-third of the cornea. Early recognition and vitamin A supplementation can prevent progression to corneal ulceration and blindness.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • X1A → conjunctival xerosis

  • X1B → Bitot’s spots

  • X2 → corneal xerosis

  • X3 → corneal ulceration/keratomalacia

Exam Pearl:
X1A is the WHO code for conjunctival xerosis in vitamin A deficiency.

Model Test-2.question: ৪১) According to British hypertension society what is the range of high normal systolic blood pressure?
Model Test-2.exp:
According to the British Hypertension Society (BHS) classification, high normal systolic blood pressure is defined as 130–139 mmHg. This range represents blood pressure above optimal levels but not yet in the hypertensive range. Systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg is classified as hypertension. Identifying patients with high-normal blood pressure is important because they have an increased risk of developing future hypertension and cardiovascular disease, requiring lifestyle modification and monitoring.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Optimal BP: <120 mmHg systolic

  • High normal systolic BP: 130–139 mmHg

  • Hypertension: ≥140 mmHg systolic

  • Lifestyle modification is recommended for high-normal BP

Exam Pearl:
BHS high normal systolic BP = 130–139 mmHg.

Model Test-2.question: ৪২) Round radio-opaque shadow with air fluid level indicates....?
Model Test-2.exp:
A round radio-opaque shadow with an air-fluid level on chest X-ray is the characteristic feature of a lung abscess. It occurs due to a localized collection of pus within the lung parenchyma, producing a cavity containing both air above and fluid (pus) below, creating an air-fluid level. Pneumonia usually shows lobar consolidation with an air bronchogram. Bronchiectasis shows features such as tram-track and signet-ring signs, while bronchial malignancy may produce a mass lesion but typically does not show a classic air-fluid level.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Lung abscess → cavity + air-fluid level

  • Pneumonia → consolidation + air bronchogram

  • Bronchiectasis → tram-track/signet-ring sign

  • Lung abscess commonly follows aspiration or bacterial infection

Exam Pearl:
Air-fluid level in a round lung opacity = lung abscess until proven otherwise.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৩) In examination of a hypertensive patient, you got abdominal bruits. What may be the underlying cause?
Model Test-2.exp:
An abdominal bruit in a patient with hypertension suggests turbulent blood flow, most commonly due to renal artery stenosis. Narrowing of the renal artery causes reduced renal perfusion, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to secondary hypertension. Abdominal bruits are an important clinical clue, especially in younger patients or those with resistant hypertension. Coarctation of the aorta may cause upper limb hypertension but is associated with radio-femoral delay and murmurs. Polycystic kidney disease and Cushing syndrome can cause hypertension but do not typically produce abdominal bruits.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Abdominal bruit + hypertension → renal artery stenosis

  • Renal artery stenosis → ↑ renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone

  • Resistant hypertension → consider secondary causes

Exam Pearl:
A hypertensive patient with an abdominal bruit classically suggests renal artery stenosis.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৪) Which type of cirrhosis is common in alcoholics?
Model Test-2.exp:
The most common type of cirrhosis associated with chronic alcohol abuse is micronodular cirrhosis (also called Laennec’s cirrhosis). It is characterized by uniform regenerative nodules usually less than 3 mm in diameter, with fibrous septa formation. Chronic alcohol intake causes hepatocyte injury, inflammation, and impaired regeneration, leading to this pattern. With disease progression, micronodules may become larger, producing a mixed nodular pattern. Macronodular cirrhosis is more commonly associated with chronic viral hepatitis and other causes of hepatocellular injury.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Alcoholic cirrhosis → micronodular (Laennec type)

  • Viral hepatitis cirrhosis → commonly macronodular

  • Micronodules: <3 mm

  • Mixed nodularity can occur in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis

Exam Pearl:
Alcoholic cirrhosis classically produces micronodular cirrhosis.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৫) Which bronchial carcinoma is most common?
Model Test-2.exp:
The most common type of bronchial carcinoma (lung cancer) overall is adenocarcinoma. It is the most frequent subtype of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) and occurs commonly in the peripheral regions of the lung. It is also the most common lung cancer type in non-smokers. Previously, squamous cell carcinoma was the most common type, especially among smokers, but adenocarcinoma has become more prevalent. Small cell carcinoma is strongly associated with smoking and has high metastatic potential but is less common overall.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common bronchial carcinoma overall → Adenocarcinoma

  • Most common NSCLC subtype → Adenocarcinoma

  • Small cell carcinoma → strong association with smoking, neuroendocrine tumor

  • Squamous cell carcinoma → central location, PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia

Exam Pearl:
Adenocarcinoma is now the most common type of bronchial carcinoma worldwide.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৬) Evidence of retinal ischemia is found at which grade of hypertensive retinopathy?
Model Test-2.exp:
Evidence of retinal ischemia appears in Grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy (Keith-Wagener-Barker classification). Grade 3 is characterized by signs of severe vascular damage including flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots (retinal infarcts due to ischemia), and hard exudates. Grade 1 shows mild arteriolar narrowing, while Grade 2 shows arteriovenous (AV) nicking and more generalized arteriolar changes. Grade 4 includes Grade 3 changes plus papilledema, indicating malignant hypertension.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Grade 1 → arteriolar narrowing

  • Grade 2 → AV nicking + arteriolar sclerosis

  • Grade 3 → hemorrhage, exudates, cotton wool spots (ischemia)

  • Grade 4 → Grade 3 + papilledema

Exam Pearl:
Cotton wool spots are signs of retinal ischemia and are a feature of Grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৭) Blood mixed vomiting is called....?
Model Test-2.exp:
Hematemesis refers to vomiting of blood, usually due to bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract (above the ligament of Treitz). The blood may appear as bright red blood or coffee-ground vomitus due to partial digestion by gastric acid. Common causes include peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, esophageal varices, and Mallory-Weiss tear. Hemoptysis is coughing up blood from the respiratory tract, melena is passage of black tarry stool due to upper GI bleeding, and hematochezia is passage of fresh blood per rectum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Hematemesis → vomiting blood

  • Hemoptysis → coughing blood

  • Melena → black tarry stool

  • Hematochezia → fresh rectal bleeding

Exam Pearl:
Blood in vomit = hematemesis (upper GI bleeding).

Model Test-2.question: ৪৮) Which one is confirmatory investigation in CLD?
Model Test-2.exp:
The confirmatory investigation for chronic liver disease (CLD) is liver biopsy, which provides direct assessment of liver architecture and can confirm the presence and severity of fibrosis, inflammation, and cirrhosis. LFT can indicate liver dysfunction but cannot confirm CLD or determine the degree of fibrosis. Viral markers help identify specific causes such as hepatitis B or C but do not confirm the extent of liver damage. CT scan and ultrasound can suggest cirrhosis through features like nodular liver and portal hypertension but are not definitive.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Liver biopsy → gold standard for diagnosis and staging of CLD

  • LFT → assesses liver function, not structural damage

  • Viral markers → identify etiology

  • Imaging → supportive evidence of cirrhosis

Exam Pearl:
Histological confirmation of chronic liver disease is done by liver biopsy.

Model Test-2.question: ৪৯) Which of the following is a feature of predominant hypertriglyceridemia?
Model Test-2.exp:
Predominant hypertriglyceridemia is associated with deposition of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (mainly chylomicrons and VLDL) in tissues, producing eruptive xanthomas. These appear as multiple small yellow papules, commonly over the extensor surfaces, buttocks, and areas exposed to pressure. Tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus are classically associated with hypercholesterolemia, especially familial hypercholesterolemia due to elevated LDL cholesterol. Prepatellar xanthoma is not a typical feature of predominant hypertriglyceridemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Hypertriglyceridemia → eruptive xanthoma

  • Familial hypercholesterolemia → tendon xanthoma + corneal arcus

  • Triglyceride-rich particles → chylomicrons and VLDL

Exam Pearl:
Eruptive xanthoma is the classic skin m

Model Test-2.question: ৫০) All of the followings are GIT causes of chronic diarrhea except..?
Model Test-2.exp:
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder and is not considered an organic cause of chronic diarrhea. It occurs due to altered gut–brain interaction and intestinal motility changes, without structural inflammation or tissue damage. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), intestinal tuberculosis, and colonic malignancy are organic GIT causes of chronic diarrhea. These conditions cause diarrhea through mechanisms such as intestinal inflammation, mucosal damage, malabsorption, or altered bowel function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Organic causes of chronic diarrhea → IBD, intestinal TB, malignancy

  • IBS → functional disorder

  • Alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, anemia) suggest organic disease

Exam Pearl:
IBS causes diarrhea but is not an organic GIT cause of chronic diarrhea.
